## Choose **one** prompt to answer

> 

> **Prompt B:** `r params$p2`

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Response

If I'm analyzing a survey dataset and I notice some responses are missing or formatted weirdly, I know I could just delete those responses, try to fill in values, or recode so everything fits more neatly. However, the route I take should depend on a few important factors–and I need to worry about how these choices affect the honesty and transparency of the research. First, I'd check why responses are missing or look strange. Sometimes missing data comes from random mistakes, but other times it's non-random: maybe certain types of people skip sensitive questions, or a poorly written question confused a lot of the respondents. If the missing information seems random and affects only a tiny fraction of the sample, I might consider removing those cases. That's simpler and avoids making assumptions about what the missing answers should have been. But if the missing data is more systematic–or if deleting cases would shrink the sample too much– then deletion could bias the results. Second, I could consider imputation– estimating a value based on other answers or using averages/modes for missing values. That can help preserve sample size, but it also introduces assumptions. Imputed values aren't real responses; treating them as if they were real can distort the data. Third, if categories are inconsistent or formatting is messy, I might clean them up by standardizing formats or recoding categories to make the analysis easier– as long as I preserve meaning and don't misrepresent people's answers. That's part of the normal data-cleaning process. What should guide my decision is transparency, logic, and fairness. I must document what I change and why to avoid hiding or changing data just to make the results look better and try to minimize bias. Good data cleaning means being honest about limitations, keeping raw data copies, and explaining what I removed or imputed. Therefore, data cleaning matters a lot– but choices on deletion, imputation, or recoding affect how trustworthy the results are. Handling missing or messy data carefully and transparently helps ensure that conclusions drawn from the survey remain honest and defensible.

## Word Count & Range Check

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
get_response_text <- function() {
  f <- knitr::current_input()
  if (is.null(f) || !file.exists(f)) return("")
  x <- readLines(f, warn = FALSE)
  # Find the lines that EXACTLY match the start/end markers
  s <- grep("^<!-- RESPONSE-START -->$", x)
  e <- grep("^<!-- RESPONSE-END -->$", x)
  if (length(s) != 1 || length(e) != 1 || e <= s) return("")
  paste(x[(s + 1L):(e - 1L)], collapse = "\n")
}
count_words <- function(txt) {
  # Remove code blocks and inline code before counting
  txt <- gsub("```[\\s\\S]*?```", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  txt <- gsub("`[^`]*`", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  # Keep letters, numbers, spaces, hyphens, and apostrophes
  txt <- gsub("[^\\p{L}\\p{N}\\s'-]", " ", txt, perl = TRUE)
  # Split by whitespace and count non-empty words
  words <- unlist(strsplit(txt, "\\s+", perl = TRUE))
  words <- words[nzchar(words)]
  length(words)
}
txt <- get_response_text()
n <- count_words(txt)
minw <- as.integer(params$word_min)
maxw <- as.integer(params$word_max)
in_range <- n >= minw && n <= maxw
cat(sprintf("**Word count:** %d  \n", n))
cat(sprintf("**Required range (%s):** %d–%d words  \n",
            toupper(params$course), minw, maxw))
cat(if (in_range) "**Status:** ✅ In range\n" else "**Status:** ❌ Out of range\n")
```
